questions.stem: Which change is a substitution mutation?

options.text: One nucleotide is replaced by another nucleotide
options.why: A substitution exchanges one nucleotide for another without changing the number of nucleotides.

options.text: One nucleotide is added between two existing nucleotides
options.why: That describes an insertion. The DNA sequence gains a nucleotide.

options.text: One nucleotide is removed from the DNA sequence
options.why: That describes a deletion. The DNA sequence loses a nucleotide.

options.text: One chromosome fails to separate during cell division
options.why: That describes nondisjunction, a chromosome-separation error rather than a base substitution.

questions.stem: Why can a base substitution in a coding sequence leave the polypeptide unchanged?

options.text: Several codons can specify the same amino acid
options.why: The genetic code is degenerate, so the changed codon may still specify the original amino acid.

options.text: Ribosomes replace any altered nucleotide during translation
options.why: Ribosomes read mRNA codons; they don’t repair altered DNA or replace nucleotides.

options.text: Every amino acid is specified by one unique codon
options.why: That contradicts degeneracy. Most amino acids are specified by more than one codon.

options.text: Substitutions always occur outside protein-coding sequences
options.why: Substitutions can occur within coding or non-coding DNA. Their location affects their possible consequences.

questions.stem: Three consecutive nucleotides are deleted from the middle of a coding sequence. What is the most direct consequence?

options.text: One amino acid is removed without shifting the downstream reading frame
options.why: Three nucleotides make one codon, so their deletion stays in frame while removing an amino acid.

options.text: Every downstream codon is regrouped because the reading frame shifts
options.why: A deletion of three bases is divisible by three, so it doesn’t shift the downstream reading frame.

options.text: One nucleotide is exchanged and may produce a synonymous mutation
options.why: That describes a substitution. This sequence has lost three nucleotides.

options.text: Translation always stops at the exact position of the deletion
options.why: An in-frame deletion doesn’t automatically create a stop codon. Translation can continue with an altered polypeptide.

questions.stem: Why can a one-base deletion near the start of a coding sequence have a large effect?

options.text: It changes the grouping of many downstream codons
options.why: The one-base deletion causes a frameshift, so codons downstream are read in a different grouping.

options.text: It replaces every base in the gene with another base
options.why: The bases remain present apart from the deleted one. Their grouping into codons changes.

options.text: It prevents the DNA molecule from being replicated anywhere
options.why: A small deletion doesn’t automatically stop replication of the whole DNA molecule.

options.text: It removes one chromosome from every cell in the organism
options.why: That describes a chromosome-number change, not a one-base deletion within a gene.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes a mutagen?

options.text: It increases the rate at which mutations occur
options.why: A mutagen raises mutation probability. Ultraviolet radiation and some chemicals are examples.

options.text: It directs a beneficial mutation to a required gene
options.why: Mutagens don’t choose changes according to an organism’s needs. They increase the chance of mutation.

options.text: It repairs errors produced during DNA replication
options.why: DNA-repair systems correct some errors. A mutagen increases DNA change or damage instead.

options.text: It guarantees that every exposed cell becomes cancerous
options.why: Mutagen exposure raises mutation risk but doesn’t guarantee cancer in every exposed cell.

questions.stem: What does the randomness of mutation mean?

options.text: Mutations don’t arise purposefully in response to an organism’s needs
options.why: Mutation isn’t directed toward producing an advantageous trait. Selection acts on variants after they arise.

options.text: Every nucleotide in every genome has an identical mutation probability
options.why: Mutation probabilities can differ among bases and regions. Randomness doesn’t require equal probabilities.

options.text: Environmental mutagens cannot affect the mutation rate
options.why: Radiation and chemical mutagens can increase mutation rates without directing a particular useful change.

options.text: Every mutation produces an unpredictable amino acid sequence
options.why: Some mutations occur outside coding regions, and synonymous substitutions don’t change the amino acid sequence.

questions.stem: A mutation occurs in a skin cell and promotes uncontrolled cell division. Which outcome is most likely?

options.text: A clone of mutant somatic cells may contribute to cancer
options.why: The mutation can pass to descendant skin cells by mitosis and promote growth of a mutant cell clone.

options.text: Every offspring will inherit the mutation through the gametes
options.why: A skin cell is somatic and doesn’t produce gametes, so its mutation normally isn’t inherited.

options.text: The mutation will immediately enter every cell in the body
options.why: A somatic mutation remains in that cell lineage. It doesn’t spread into all other body cells.

options.text: Natural selection will remove the mutation before the cell divides
options.why: There’s no guarantee that the cell will be removed. Mutant cells can survive and produce a clone.

questions.stem: Why is mutation the original source of genetic variation?

options.text: It creates new DNA sequences and therefore new alleles
options.why: Mutation produces new sequence variants. Other processes can then rearrange or alter the frequencies of those variants.

options.text: It sorts existing alleles into different gamete combinations
options.why: That describes independent assortment and recombination during sexual reproduction, which rearrange existing alleles.

options.text: It increases beneficial allele frequencies in every environment
options.why: Natural selection can change allele frequencies. Mutation creates alleles without guaranteeing that they’re beneficial.

options.text: It causes each organism to acquire traits during its lifetime
options.why: Acquired traits aren’t the source of inherited sequence variation. Heritable mutation must affect the germline.

questions.stem: What conclusion can be drawn when a gene-knockout organism differs from an otherwise similar control?

options.text: The inactivated gene probably contributes to the altered process
options.why: The controlled difference provides evidence that the gene has a role in the affected phenotype or process.

options.text: The inactivated gene is the only gene involved in the process
options.why: Other genes and indirect effects may contribute. A knockout doesn’t show that one gene acts alone.

options.text: Every nucleotide in the inactivated gene has been deleted
options.why: A knockout only requires the gene to become inoperative. The entire sequence doesn’t have to be removed.

options.text: The altered phenotype must be beneficial in natural environments
options.why: A knockout identifies a functional effect, not whether that effect improves reproductive success.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly identifies the roles of guide RNA and Cas9?

options.text: Guide RNA binds complementary target DNA; Cas9 cuts the DNA
options.why: Complementary base pairing directs the complex to the target, and Cas9 acts as the nuclease.

options.text: Guide RNA cuts the DNA; Cas9 supplies a replacement chromosome
options.why: Guide RNA isn’t a nuclease, and Cas9 doesn’t provide a chromosome. Cas9 performs the cut.

options.text: Guide RNA repairs the DNA; Cas9 translates the edited gene
options.why: Cellular enzymes repair the cut, while ribosomes perform translation. Neither role is described here accurately.

options.text: Guide RNA copies the gene; Cas9 carries amino acids to ribosomes
options.why: DNA replication enzymes copy DNA, and tRNAs carry amino acids. CRISPR-Cas9 targets and cuts DNA.

questions.stem: Why does editing an embryo or germline raise a concern that somatic editing usually doesn’t?

options.text: The edit could be inherited by future generations
options.why: A germline edit can enter gametes and descendants, affecting people who couldn’t consent to the original procedure.

options.text: The edit cannot change any DNA sequence in the treated cells
options.why: Both germline and somatic editing can change DNA. The difference here is potential inheritance.

options.text: The edit always causes cancer in the treated organism
options.why: Gene editing can have risks, but cancer isn’t an unavoidable outcome of every edit.

options.text: The edit affects proteins but leaves all genes unchanged
options.why: Gene editing alters DNA, which may then change gene expression or the protein produced.

questions.stem: Which observation best supports functional constraint as an explanation for a highly conserved sequence?

options.text: Sequence changes reduce function and are removed by selection
options.why: If variants reduce fitness, purifying selection removes them and preserves the functional sequence over time.

options.text: The sequence accumulates neutral substitutions faster than surrounding DNA
options.why: Rapid accumulation would produce divergence rather than strong conservation.

options.text: The sequence is copied without any possibility of mutation
options.why: Conserved sequences can mutate. Their variants may arise slowly or be removed by selection.

options.text: The sequence occurs only in one recently formed population
options.why: High conservation is similarity maintained over long evolutionary periods, often across species.
